name: SSC Tense and Verb Form Errors
description: Tense, verb form, gerund, infinitive, and modal verb error patterns for SSC English.

cards.term: Error: He has went home
cards.definition:
Correct: He has gone home

Rule: After has, have, or had, use the past participle V3.

Example: He has gone home, probably after pretending he understood the whole lecture.

cards.term: Error: They have ate lunch
cards.definition:
Correct: They have eaten lunch

Rule: Have plus past participle is required in present perfect.

Example: They have eaten lunch, but the tiffin boxes still smell like evidence.

cards.term: Error: She had saw the movie
cards.definition:
Correct: She had seen the movie

Rule: Had is followed by V3, not V2.

Example: She had seen the movie before everyone started giving spoilers.

cards.term: Error: I have wrote the answer
cards.definition:
Correct: I have written the answer

Rule: Use V3 after have.

Example: I have written the answer so neatly that even my future self can read it.

cards.term: Error: We had drank the water
cards.definition:
Correct: We had drunk the water

Rule: Had takes the past participle form.

Example: We had drunk the water before noticing the bottle was labelled for guests.

cards.term: Error: He has broke the glass
cards.definition:
Correct: He has broken the glass

Rule: Present perfect uses has or have plus V3.

Example: He has broken the glass and is now blaming physics.

cards.term: Error: She has forgot her password
cards.definition:
Correct: She has forgotten her password

Rule: Use the past participle after has.

Example: She has forgotten her password, but remembers every embarrassing school incident.

cards.term: Error: They have began the work
cards.definition:
Correct: They have begun the work

Rule: Present perfect requires V3.

Example: They have begun the work, which is already better than only discussing it.

cards.term: Error: He had took my pen
cards.definition:
Correct: He had taken my pen

Rule: Had must be followed by V3.

Example: He had taken my pen and somehow also my trust.

cards.term: Error: She has chose the right option
cards.definition:
Correct: She has chosen the right option

Rule: Use chosen after has or have.

Example: She has chosen the right option with the confidence of a topper.

cards.term: Error: I have gave him the book
cards.definition:
Correct: I have given him the book

Rule: Give becomes given after have.

Example: I have given him the book, and now he has no excuse.

cards.term: Error: He has ran fast
cards.definition:
Correct: He has run fast

Rule: Run remains run as V3.

Example: He has run fast enough to escape morning exercise.

cards.term: Error: She had spoke clearly
cards.definition:
Correct: She had spoken clearly

Rule: Speak becomes spoken in perfect tense.

Example: She had spoken clearly, but the microphone chose rebellion.

cards.term: Error: The bell has rang
cards.definition:
Correct: The bell has rung

Rule: Ring becomes rung after has or have.

Example: The bell has rung, and suddenly every student respects punctuality.

cards.term: Error: He has drove the car
cards.definition:
Correct: He has driven the car

Rule: Drive becomes driven in perfect tense.

Example: He has driven the car carefully, which shocked the entire family.

cards.term: Error: They have swam across the river
cards.definition:
Correct: They have swum across the river

Rule: Swim becomes swum after have.

Example: They have swum across the river like the bridge personally offended them.

cards.term: Error: She has sang well
cards.definition:
Correct: She has sung well

Rule: Sing becomes sung after has.

Example: She has sung well enough to make the neighbours forgive the practice sessions.

cards.term: Error: He had fell down
cards.definition:
Correct: He had fallen down

Rule: Fall becomes fallen after had.

Example: He had fallen down, but stood up like a motivational poster.

cards.term: Error: I have knew him for years
cards.definition:
Correct: I have known him for years

Rule: Know becomes known in perfect tense.

Example: I have known him for years and still cannot understand his ringtone choice.

cards.term: Error: She has wore a blue dress
cards.definition:
Correct: She has worn a blue dress

Rule: Wear becomes worn after has.

Example: She has worn a blue dress that made even the dull room look planned.

cards.term: Error: He did not went there
cards.definition:
Correct: He did not go there

Rule: Did is followed by base form V1.

Example: He did not go there, although his excuse travelled everywhere.

cards.term: Error: She did not came today
cards.definition:
Correct: She did not come today

Rule: After did not, use base verb.

Example: She did not come today, and the group project collapsed emotionally.

cards.term: Error: Did you saw him?
cards.definition:
Correct: Did you see him?

Rule: Did plus subject is followed by V1.

Example: Did you see him, or did he vanish like a good Wi-Fi signal?

cards.term: Error: Did they completed the task?
cards.definition:
Correct: Did they complete the task?

Rule: Use base verb after did.

Example: Did they complete the task before the deadline, or before the panic?

cards.term: Error: I did not understood the rule
cards.definition:
Correct: I did not understand the rule

Rule: Did not is followed by V1.

Example: I did not understand the rule until the wrong answer hurt my marks.

cards.term: Error: He does not likes tea
cards.definition:
Correct: He does not like tea

Rule: Does not is followed by base verb.

Example: He does not like tea, which is treated like a scandal in some families.

cards.term: Error: She does not knows the answer
cards.definition:
Correct: She does not know the answer

Rule: After does not, use V1.

Example: She does not know the answer, but her confident face is doing overtime.

cards.term: Error: Does he goes to school?
cards.definition:
Correct: Does he go to school?

Rule: Does is followed by base verb.

Example: Does he go to school, or only to the canteen?

cards.term: Error: It does not works
cards.definition:
Correct: It does not work

Rule: Use V1 after does not.

Example: It does not work, and restarting it has become a religious ritual.

cards.term: Error: The machine does not starts
cards.definition:
Correct: The machine does not start

Rule: Does not takes base verb.

Example: The machine does not start unless someone threatens to replace it.

cards.term: Error: He don't like coffee
cards.definition:
Correct: He doesn't like coffee

Rule: Use does not with singular third person.

Example: He doesn't like coffee, but still behaves like he has had three cups.

cards.term: Error: She don't understand
cards.definition:
Correct: She doesn't understand

Rule: Singular third person uses does not.

Example: She doesn't understand why the answer key disagrees with her confidence.

cards.term: Error: It don't matter
cards.definition:
Correct: It doesn't matter

Rule: “It” takes does not, not do not.

Example: It doesn't matter now, but it mattered loudly five minutes ago.

cards.term: Error: They doesn't agree
cards.definition:
Correct: They don't agree

Rule: Plural subject takes do not.

Example: They don't agree, which means the meeting has just begun.

cards.term: Error: We doesn't need help
cards.definition:
Correct: We don't need help

Rule: “We” takes do not.

Example: We don't need help, said the group just before asking for help.

cards.term: Error: I doesn't know
cards.definition:
Correct: I don't know

Rule: “I” takes do not.

Example: I don't know is sometimes the most honest answer in the room.

cards.term: Error: He go to school daily
cards.definition:
Correct: He goes to school daily

Rule: In simple present, singular third person takes s or es.

Example: He goes to school daily, unless rain offers a dramatic excuse.

cards.term: Error: She teach English
cards.definition:
Correct: She teaches English

Rule: Add es to verbs ending in ch, sh, s, x, or o for singular third person.

Example: She teaches English with the energy of a courtroom lawyer.

cards.term: Error: The sun rise in the east
cards.definition:
Correct: The sun rises in the east

Rule: Universal truths use simple present with correct subject agreement.

Example: The sun rises in the east, even on days when students rise late.

cards.term: Error: My brother play cricket
cards.definition:
Correct: My brother plays cricket

Rule: Singular third person in simple present takes s.

Example: My brother plays cricket as if the street is Wankhede Stadium.

cards.term: Error: The dog bark at night
cards.definition:
Correct: The dog barks at night

Rule: Singular subject takes singular verb in simple present.

Example: The dog barks at night like it has breaking news.

cards.term: Error: Birds flies in the sky
cards.definition:
Correct: Birds fly in the sky

Rule: Plural subjects take base verb in simple present.

Example: Birds fly in the sky without needing a timetable.

cards.term: Error: Children plays outside
cards.definition:
Correct: Children play outside

Rule: Plural subject takes base verb.

Example: Children play outside while adults discuss screen time.

cards.term: Error: The boys goes to school
cards.definition:
Correct: The boys go to school

Rule: Plural subject takes V1.

Example: The boys go to school, but their minds may still be at the playground.

cards.term: Error: I am knowing the answer
cards.definition:
Correct: I know the answer

Rule: Stative verbs like know are usually not used in continuous tense.

Example: I know the answer, though my face is pretending otherwise.

cards.term: Error: She is having a car
cards.definition:
Correct: She has a car

Rule: Have meaning possession is not normally used in continuous form.

Example: She has a car, and every cousin suddenly has travel plans.

cards.term: Error: He is believing in hard work
cards.definition:
Correct: He believes in hard work

Rule: Believe is a stative verb and usually takes simple present.

Example: He believes in hard work, especially when others are doing it.

cards.term: Error: I am liking this song
cards.definition:
Correct: I like this song

Rule: Like is generally a stative verb.

Example: I like this song enough to replay it until everyone else dislikes it.

cards.term: Error: She is seeming tired
cards.definition:
Correct: She seems tired

Rule: Seem is a stative verb.

Example: She seems tired because the meeting had three conclusions and no ending.

cards.term: Error: This curry is tasting good
cards.definition:
Correct: This curry tastes good

Rule: Taste as a state or quality usually takes simple present.

Example: This curry tastes good enough to make silence at the table.

cards.term: Error: The flower is smelling sweet
cards.definition:
Correct: The flower smells sweet

Rule: Smell as a quality uses simple present.

Example: The flower smells sweet, unlike the school shoes nearby.

cards.term: Error: I am remembering his name
cards.definition:
Correct: I remember his name

Rule: Remember is generally a stative verb.

Example: I remember his name but not where I kept my notes.

cards.term: Error: She is owning two houses
cards.definition:
Correct: She owns two houses

Rule: Own is a stative verb.

Example: She owns two houses and still complains about cupboard space.

cards.term: Error: I am understanding the topic
cards.definition:
Correct: I understand the topic

Rule: Understand is normally stative.

Example: I understand the topic now, which is exactly when the teacher changes the question.

cards.term: Error: He is seeing the problem now
cards.definition:
Correct: He sees the problem now

Rule: See meaning understand or perceive is usually stative.

Example: He sees the problem now, after creating half of it.

cards.term: Error: I am hearing a sound
cards.definition:
Correct: I hear a sound

Rule: Hear as involuntary perception is normally stative.

Example: I hear a sound that suspiciously resembles my phone falling.

cards.term: Error: She is wanting a new phone
cards.definition:
Correct: She wants a new phone

Rule: Want is a stative verb.

Example: She wants a new phone because the old one has developed a personality.

cards.term: Error: He is needing help
cards.definition:
Correct: He needs help

Rule: Need is normally not used in continuous tense.

Example: He needs help, but his ego is still buffering.

cards.term: Error: I am preferring tea
cards.definition:
Correct: I prefer tea

Rule: Prefer is generally stative.

Example: I prefer tea, especially when coffee tastes like burnt ambition.

cards.term: Error: I am agreeing with you
cards.definition:
Correct: I agree with you

Rule: Agree is usually a stative verb.

Example: I agree with you, which is rare enough to record.

cards.term: Error: He is belonging to this village
cards.definition:
Correct: He belongs to this village

Rule: Belong is a stative verb.

Example: He belongs to this village and knows every shortcut through it.

cards.term: Error: She is resembling her mother
cards.definition:
Correct: She resembles her mother

Rule: Resemble is normally stative.

Example: She resembles her mother so much that old neighbours greet her twice.

cards.term: Error: I am thinking you are right
cards.definition:
Correct: I think you are right

Rule: Think meaning believe is stative.

Example: I think you are right, but my pride needs two minutes to accept it.

cards.term: Error: I have visited Delhi yesterday
cards.definition:
Correct: I visited Delhi yesterday

Rule: Use simple past with a finished past time such as yesterday.

Example: I visited Delhi yesterday and learned that traffic has its own personality.

cards.term: Error: She has called me last night
cards.definition:
Correct: She called me last night

Rule: Use simple past with definite past time expressions.

Example: She called me last night just when my phone was at one percent.

cards.term: Error: They have completed it in 2020
cards.definition:
Correct: They completed it in 2020

Rule: Use simple past with a specific finished past year.

Example: They completed it in 2020, a year everyone remembers for other reasons.

cards.term: Error: I have met him two days ago
cards.definition:
Correct: I met him two days ago

Rule: “Ago” requires simple past, not present perfect.

Example: I met him two days ago and forgot his name yesterday.

cards.term: Error: He has left an hour ago
cards.definition:
Correct: He left an hour ago

Rule: Use simple past with “ago”.

Example: He left an hour ago, but his perfume is still in the room.

cards.term: Error: We have watched the match last Sunday
cards.definition:
Correct: We watched the match last Sunday

Rule: Specific past time takes simple past.

Example: We watched the match last Sunday and lost our voices by evening.

cards.term: Error: She has bought this pen yesterday
cards.definition:
Correct: She bought this pen yesterday

Rule: Yesterday takes simple past.

Example: She bought this pen yesterday, and today it has already disappeared.

cards.term: Error: I saw him just now
cards.definition:
Correct: I have just seen him

Rule: With just in British/Indian exam style, present perfect is often preferred for a very recent action.

Example: I have just seen him near the gate, moving like he forgot homework.

cards.term: Error: He just completed the work
cards.definition:
Correct: He has just completed the work

Rule: “Just” for recent completion usually takes present perfect in formal usage.

Example: He has just completed the work after calling it easy for three hours.

cards.term: Error: I am living here since 2020
cards.definition:
Correct: I have been living here since 2020

Rule: Use present perfect continuous for an action continuing from the past to now.

Example: I have been living here since 2020, long enough to know every noisy neighbour.

cards.term: Error: She is studying for two hours
cards.definition:
Correct: She has been studying for two hours

Rule: Use present perfect continuous with for plus duration continuing to present.

Example: She has been studying for two hours, and even the chair looks tired.

cards.term: Error: He works here since May
cards.definition:
Correct: He has worked here since May

Rule: Use present perfect for a state/action continuing from the past.

Example: He has worked here since May and already knows the tea schedule.

cards.term: Error: They live here since childhood
cards.definition:
Correct: They have lived here since childhood

Rule: Since plus starting point with continuing action takes present perfect.

Example: They have lived here since childhood and know which shop gives extra chutney.

cards.term: Error: I know him since 2015
cards.definition:
Correct: I have known him since 2015

Rule: Know is stative and uses present perfect for continuing state.

Example: I have known him since 2015 and still cannot predict his excuses.

cards.term: Error: She is waiting for an hour
cards.definition:
Correct: She has been waiting for an hour

Rule: Use present perfect continuous for waiting that began in past and continues now.

Example: She has been waiting for an hour, which is now a separate personality test.

cards.term: Error: It rains since morning
cards.definition:
Correct: It has been raining since morning

Rule: Use present perfect continuous for an action continuing from a past point.

Example: It has been raining since morning, and the road has become a mirror.

cards.term: Error: He is sleeping since afternoon
cards.definition:
Correct: He has been sleeping since afternoon

Rule: Since plus starting point takes present perfect continuous.

Example: He has been sleeping since afternoon like a phone on airplane mode.

cards.term: Error: We are playing for two hours
cards.definition:
Correct: We have been playing for two hours

Rule: For plus duration continuing to present takes present perfect continuous.

Example: We have been playing for two hours, and the ball has more energy than us.

cards.term: Error: I have been knowing him for years
cards.definition:
Correct: I have known him for years

Rule: Stative verbs like know use present perfect, not perfect continuous.

Example: I have known him for years, which explains my patience.

cards.term: Error: She has been having this car for five years
cards.definition:
Correct: She has had this car for five years

Rule: Have meaning possession uses present perfect, not perfect continuous.

Example: She has had this car for five years, and the seat cover tells the history.

cards.term: Error: He has been owning this shop since 2019
cards.definition:
Correct: He has owned this shop since 2019

Rule: Own is stative, so use present perfect.

Example: He has owned this shop since 2019 and knows every bargaining style.

cards.term: Error: I have been believing this for years
cards.definition:
Correct: I have believed this for years

Rule: Believe is stative.

Example: I have believed this for years, though facts are now knocking loudly.

cards.term: Error: When I reached, he left
cards.definition:
Correct: When I reached, he had left

Rule: Use past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.

Example: When I reached, he had left, which is the official beginning of my villain story.

cards.term: Error: The train left before we reached
cards.definition:
Correct: The train had left before we reached

Rule: Earlier past action takes had plus V3.

Example: The train had left before we reached, because punctuality chose the train.

cards.term: Error: She cooked dinner before I arrived
cards.definition:
Correct: She had cooked dinner before I arrived

Rule: Use past perfect for the earlier completed action.

Example: She had cooked dinner before I arrived, saving everyone from my cooking.

cards.term: Error: He finished the work before the boss came
cards.definition:
Correct: He had finished the work before the boss came

Rule: Earlier action in the past takes past perfect.

Example: He had finished the work before the boss came, which looked suspiciously efficient.

cards.term: Error: The patient died before the doctor arrived
cards.definition:
Correct: The patient had died before the doctor arrived

Rule: Earlier past event takes had plus V3.

Example: The patient had died before the doctor arrived in the tragic report.

cards.term: Error: I never saw such a place before
cards.definition:
Correct: I had never seen such a place before

Rule: Before a later past reference, use past perfect for earlier experience.

Example: I had never seen such a place before, unless dreams count.

cards.term: Error: After he finished the work, he went home
cards.definition:
Correct: After he had finished the work, he went home

Rule: Past perfect may be used after after to show the earlier completed action.

Example: After he had finished the work, he went home like a liberated prisoner.

cards.term: Error: I will call you when I will reach home
cards.definition:
Correct: I will call you when I reach home

Rule: In time clauses with when, use present tense for future meaning.

Example: I will call you when I reach home, unless the phone dies dramatically.

cards.term: Error: She will inform us after she will arrive
cards.definition:
Correct: She will inform us after she arrives

Rule: Use simple present in future time clauses after after, when, until, before.

Example: She will inform us after she arrives, probably with three missed calls first.

cards.term: Error: Wait here until I will return
cards.definition:
Correct: Wait here until I return

Rule: Use present tense after until for future time.

Example: Wait here until I return, said every parent in every market.

cards.term: Error: I will start before he will come
cards.definition:
Correct: I will start before he comes

Rule: Future time clauses use present tense.

Example: I will start before he comes, because waiting for him is a lifestyle.

cards.term: Error: We will leave as soon as the rain will stop
cards.definition:
Correct: We will leave as soon as the rain stops

Rule: Use simple present after as soon as for future meaning.

Example: We will leave as soon as the rain stops, if the road is still a road.

cards.term: Error: If he will work hard, he will pass
cards.definition:
Correct: If he works hard, he will pass

Rule: First conditional uses if plus simple present, then will plus verb.

Example: If he works hard, he will pass, and his relatives will claim they predicted it.

cards.term: Error: If it will rain, we will stay home
cards.definition:
Correct: If it rains, we will stay home

Rule: Use simple present in the if clause for real future condition.

Example: If it rains, we will stay home and call it a productivity day.

cards.term: Error: If you will study, you will improve
cards.definition:
Correct: If you study, you will improve

Rule: First conditional takes present tense after if.

Example: If you study, you will improve, which is annoyingly true.

cards.term: Error: Unless you will hurry, you will miss the train
cards.definition:
Correct: Unless you hurry, you will miss the train

Rule: Use present tense after unless for future meaning.

Example: Unless you hurry, you will miss the train and gain a story.

cards.term: Error: I wish I am rich
cards.definition:
Correct: I wish I were rich

Rule: Wish for an unreal present uses past subjunctive, often were.

Example: I wish I were rich enough to buy books without checking price tags.

cards.term: Error: I wish he comes here
cards.definition:
Correct: I wish he would come here

Rule: Wish for desired future change often uses would.

Example: I wish he would come here before the snacks disappear.

cards.term: Error: I wish I know the answer
cards.definition:
Correct: I wish I knew the answer

Rule: Wish for unreal present uses past tense.

Example: I wish I knew the answer, said every student after choosing option C.

cards.term: Error: If I was you, I would apologise
cards.definition:
Correct: If I were you, I would apologise

Rule: Unreal condition commonly uses were with all subjects.

Example: If I were you, I would apologise before the screenshot spreads.

cards.term: Error: If he would study, he would pass
cards.definition:
Correct: If he studied, he would pass

Rule: Second conditional uses if plus past tense, then would plus V1.

Example: If he studied, he would pass, but his phone keeps winning.

cards.term: Error: If I would have known, I would have helped
cards.definition:
Correct: If I had known, I would have helped

Rule: Third conditional uses if plus had V3, then would have V3.

Example: If I had known, I would have helped instead of giving useless advice.

cards.term: Error: If she came earlier, she would have met him
cards.definition:
Correct: If she had come earlier, she would have met him

Rule: Unreal past condition requires had plus V3.

Example: If she had come earlier, she would have met him before he vanished.

cards.term: Error: Had I knew this, I would act differently
cards.definition:
Correct: Had I known this, I would have acted differently

Rule: In inverted third conditional, use had plus V3 and would have plus V3.

Example: Had I known this, I would have acted differently, and saved my marks.

cards.term: Error: I would rather you go now
cards.definition:
Correct: I would rather you went now

Rule: Would rather plus subject takes past tense for present preference.

Example: I would rather you went now, before the argument becomes a documentary.

cards.term: Error: It is time you go home
cards.definition:
Correct: It is time you went home

Rule: “It is time” is followed by past tense for present/future action.

Example: It is time you went home, because even the chairs look tired.

cards.term: Error: He talks as if he knows everything
cards.definition:
Correct: He talks as if he knew everything

Rule: For unreal comparison, use past tense after as if.

Example: He talks as if he knew everything, including the examiner's mood.

cards.term: Error: She behaved as if she is the boss
cards.definition:
Correct: She behaved as if she were the boss

Rule: Unreal comparison after as if takes past subjunctive.

Example: She behaved as if she were the boss, and even the boss looked confused.

cards.term: Error: I prefer to walk than to run
cards.definition:
Correct: I prefer walking to running

Rule: Prefer is followed by to, not than, in this comparison pattern.

Example: I prefer walking to running because dignity matters.

cards.term: Error: I would prefer tea than coffee
cards.definition:
Correct: I would prefer tea to coffee

Rule: Prefer takes to, not than.

Example: I would prefer tea to coffee during late-night revision.

cards.term: Error: I prefer tea rather than coffee
cards.definition:
Correct: I prefer tea to coffee

Rule: Standard structure is prefer A to B.

Example: I prefer tea to coffee, especially when coffee tastes like burnt homework.

cards.term: Error: He made me to wait
cards.definition:
Correct: He made me wait

Rule: Make plus object takes bare infinitive.

Example: He made me wait so long that the chair and I became friends.

cards.term: Error: Let him to go
cards.definition:
Correct: Let him go

Rule: Let plus object takes bare infinitive.

Example: Let him go before he explains the same excuse again.

cards.term: Error: Help me to solve it
cards.definition:
Correct: Help me solve it

Rule: Help can take bare infinitive in common usage, though to-infinitive is also possible.

Example: Help me solve it before the calculator starts judging me.

cards.term: Error: I heard him to sing
cards.definition:
Correct: I heard him sing

Rule: Verbs of perception take bare infinitive for complete action.

Example: I heard him sing, and the neighbourhood heard him suffer.

cards.term: Error: I saw him to cross the road
cards.definition:
Correct: I saw him cross the road

Rule: See plus object takes bare infinitive for complete action.

Example: I saw him cross the road with heroic confidence and zero traffic sense.

cards.term: Error: She watched the child to play
cards.definition:
Correct: She watched the child play

Rule: Watch plus object takes bare infinitive for complete action.

Example: She watched the child play like the floor was a stadium.

cards.term: Error: I made him understood
cards.definition:
Correct: I made him understand

Rule: Make plus object takes base verb.

Example: I made him understand the rule using three pens and one biscuit.

cards.term: Error: He let me went home
cards.definition:
Correct: He let me go home

Rule: Let plus object takes base verb.

Example: He let me go home before the meeting grew another agenda.

cards.term: Error: I want that he should come
cards.definition:
Correct: I want him to come

Rule: Use want plus object plus to-infinitive.

Example: I want him to come early, which is ambitious based on history.

cards.term: Error: She told me that go there
cards.definition:
Correct: She told me to go there

Rule: Tell plus object takes to-infinitive for instructions.

Example: She told me to go there, so naturally I asked for the location after leaving.

cards.term: Error: He ordered me that I should wait
cards.definition:
Correct: He ordered me to wait

Rule: Order plus object takes to-infinitive.

Example: He ordered me to wait while he searched for the file he lost.

cards.term: Error: I suggested him to apply
cards.definition:
Correct: I suggested that he apply

Rule: Suggest is not normally followed by object plus to-infinitive.

Example: I suggested that he apply before the deadline eats the form.

cards.term: Error: She suggested me to read this book
cards.definition:
Correct: She suggested that I read this book

Rule: Use suggest plus that clause.

Example: She suggested that I read this book, and now my shelf is judging me.

cards.term: Error: He advised me that I should study
cards.definition:
Correct: He advised me to study

Rule: Advise plus object takes to-infinitive.

Example: He advised me to study, which was rude but accurate.

cards.term: Error: Avoid to make mistakes
cards.definition:
Correct: Avoid making mistakes

Rule: Avoid is followed by gerund.

Example: Avoid making mistakes, especially the ones the examiner loves.

cards.term: Error: Enjoy to read novels
cards.definition:
Correct: Enjoy reading novels

Rule: Enjoy is followed by gerund.

Example: I enjoy reading novels until the plot attacks my sleep schedule.

cards.term: Error: Stop to talk in class
cards.definition:
Correct: Stop talking in class

Rule: Stop plus gerund means end the activity.

Example: Stop talking in class before the teacher develops radar hearing.

cards.term: Error: He denied to steal the money
cards.definition:
Correct: He denied stealing the money

Rule: Deny is followed by gerund.

Example: He denied stealing the money while standing beside a very guilty pocket.

cards.term: Error: She avoided to answer
cards.definition:
Correct: She avoided answering

Rule: Avoid takes gerund.

Example: She avoided answering the question with the skill of a politician.

cards.term: Error: I dislike to wait
cards.definition:
Correct: I dislike waiting

Rule: Dislike is commonly followed by gerund.

Example: I dislike waiting, especially when the queue has philosophical patience.

cards.term: Error: He admitted to make a mistake
cards.definition:
Correct: He admitted making a mistake

Rule: Admit is followed by gerund.

Example: He admitted making a mistake, and the room briefly became peaceful.

cards.term: Error: They considered to buy a house
cards.definition:
Correct: They considered buying a house

Rule: Consider is followed by gerund.

Example: They considered buying a house, then met the property prices.

cards.term: Error: She postponed to meet him
cards.definition:
Correct: She postponed meeting him

Rule: Postpone is followed by gerund.

Example: She postponed meeting him until his excuses improved.

cards.term: Error: He finished to write the essay
cards.definition:
Correct: He finished writing the essay

Rule: Finish is followed by gerund.

Example: He finished writing the essay and then found the word limit.

cards.term: Error: I cannot resist to laugh
cards.definition:
Correct: I cannot resist laughing

Rule: Resist is followed by gerund.

Example: I cannot resist laughing when someone says “quick meeting”.

cards.term: Error: He risked to lose everything
cards.definition:
Correct: He risked losing everything

Rule: Risk is followed by gerund.

Example: He risked losing everything for a shortcut that was not short.

cards.term: Error: She practised to speak English
cards.definition:
Correct: She practised speaking English

Rule: Practise is followed by gerund.

Example: She practised speaking English by explaining cricket to a mirror.

cards.term: Error: He kept to ask questions
cards.definition:
Correct: He kept asking questions

Rule: Keep is followed by gerund for repeated action.

Example: He kept asking questions until curiosity became a public event.

cards.term: Error: I look forward to meet you
cards.definition:
Correct: I look forward to meeting you

Rule: “Look forward to” uses gerund because to is a preposition here.

Example: I look forward to meeting you, said the email with formal politeness.

cards.term: Error: He is used to work hard
cards.definition:
Correct: He is used to working hard

Rule: Be used to takes gerund.

Example: He is used to working hard, but not to working without tea.

cards.term: Error: She is accustomed to wake early
cards.definition:
Correct: She is accustomed to waking early

Rule: Accustomed to takes gerund.

Example: She is accustomed to waking early, unlike her alarm clock which is ignored.

cards.term: Error: He objected to pay the fine
cards.definition:
Correct: He objected to paying the fine

Rule: Object to takes gerund.

Example: He objected to paying the fine but not to breaking the rule.

cards.term: Error: I am interested to learn grammar
cards.definition:
Correct: I am interested in learning grammar

Rule: Interested is followed by in plus gerund.

Example: I am interested in learning grammar because marks are persuasive.

cards.term: Error: He insisted to go
cards.definition:
Correct: He insisted on going

Rule: Insist is followed by on plus gerund.

Example: He insisted on going, even though the plan had disaster written in bold.

cards.term: Error: She succeeded to pass the exam
cards.definition:
Correct: She succeeded in passing the exam

Rule: Succeed is followed by in plus gerund.

Example: She succeeded in passing the exam and suddenly became the family expert.

cards.term: Error: He prevented me to enter
cards.definition:
Correct: He prevented me from entering

Rule: Prevent is followed by object plus from plus gerund.

Example: He prevented me from entering because my ID card was at home resting.

cards.term: Error: The rain stopped us to play
cards.definition:
Correct: The rain stopped us from playing

Rule: Stop someone from doing something.

Example: The rain stopped us from playing and promoted indoor boredom.

cards.term: Error: He accused me to lie
cards.definition:
Correct: He accused me of lying

Rule: Accuse someone of doing something.

Example: He accused me of lying because the truth sounded too creative.

cards.term: Error: She blamed me to break the cup
cards.definition:
Correct: She blamed me for breaking the cup

Rule: Blame someone for doing something.

Example: She blamed me for breaking the cup, although gravity participated.

cards.term: Error: I am busy to write notes
cards.definition:
Correct: I am busy writing notes

Rule: Busy is followed by gerund.

Example: I am busy writing notes while my phone feels neglected.

cards.term: Error: It is no use to argue
cards.definition:
Correct: It is no use arguing

Rule: No use is followed by gerund.

Example: It is no use arguing with a person who treats opinion as fact.

cards.term: Error: It is worth to try
cards.definition:
Correct: It is worth trying

Rule: Worth is followed by gerund.

Example: It is worth trying, especially if the alternative is regret.

cards.term: Error: I cannot help to laugh
cards.definition:
Correct: I cannot help laughing

Rule: Cannot help is followed by gerund.

Example: I cannot help laughing when autocorrect ruins a serious message.

cards.term: Error: She is good to sing
cards.definition:
Correct: She is good at singing

Rule: Good at is followed by gerund.

Example: She is good at singing, which the neighbours confirm unwillingly.

cards.term: Error: He is fond to read
cards.definition:
Correct: He is fond of reading

Rule: Fond of is followed by gerund.

Example: He is fond of reading, even the labels on shampoo bottles.

cards.term: Error: I am tired to wait
cards.definition:
Correct: I am tired of waiting

Rule: Tired of is followed by gerund.

Example: I am tired of waiting, and the clock looks guilty.

cards.term: Error: He is capable to solve it
cards.definition:
Correct: He is capable of solving it

Rule: Capable of is followed by gerund.

Example: He is capable of solving it if he stops arguing with the question.

cards.term: Error: She is afraid to dogs
cards.definition:
Correct: She is afraid of dogs

Rule: Afraid is followed by of plus noun or gerund.

Example: She is afraid of dogs, especially the tiny ones with giant confidence.

cards.term: Error: He is afraid of go there
cards.definition:
Correct: He is afraid of going there

Rule: Preposition of takes gerund.

Example: He is afraid of going there because the last visit became a family meeting.

cards.term: Error: I used to going there
cards.definition:
Correct: I used to go there

Rule: Used to for past habit takes base verb.

Example: I used to go there when the shop sold samosas for sensible prices.

cards.term: Error: He used to played cricket
cards.definition:
Correct: He used to play cricket

Rule: Used to is followed by base verb.

Example: He used to play cricket before office files became his new sport.

cards.term: Error: She use to study at night
cards.definition:
Correct: She used to study at night

Rule: Past habit takes used to.

Example: She used to study at night when silence finally defeated noise.

cards.term: Error: Did you used to live here?
cards.definition:
Correct: Did you use to live here?

Rule: After did, use base form use.

Example: Did you use to live here before the road became a parking lot?

cards.term: Error: I am use to waking early
cards.definition:
Correct: I am used to waking early

Rule: Be used to means accustomed to.

Example: I am used to waking early, though my soul files a complaint daily.

cards.term: Error: He needs not come
cards.definition:
Correct: He need not come

Rule: Modal need not is followed by base verb and does not take s.

Example: He need not come if he plans to arrive after the work ends.

cards.term: Error: He dare not to speak
cards.definition:
Correct: He dare not speak

Rule: Modal dare not is followed by base verb.

Example: He dare not speak when the principal raises an eyebrow.

cards.term: Error: He must goes now
cards.definition:
Correct: He must go now

Rule: Modals are followed by base verb.

Example: He must go now before the bus becomes a memory.

cards.term: Error: She can sings well
cards.definition:
Correct: She can sing well

Rule: Can takes base verb.

Example: She can sing well enough to make the microphone proud.

cards.term: Error: They should works hard
cards.definition:
Correct: They should work hard

Rule: Should takes base verb.

Example: They should work hard, not just discuss strategy like experts.

cards.term: Error: He may comes today
cards.definition:
Correct: He may come today

Rule: May takes base verb.

Example: He may come today, which means we should not rely on it.

cards.term: Error: You ought work hard
cards.definition:
Correct: You ought to work hard

Rule: Ought is followed by to plus base verb.

Example: You ought to work hard because luck has limited office hours.

cards.term: Error: He had better to leave
cards.definition:
Correct: He had better leave

Rule: Had better is followed by base verb.

Example: He had better leave before the polite smiles expire.

cards.term: Error: I would rather to stay home
cards.definition:
Correct: I would rather stay home

Rule: Would rather is followed by base verb.

Example: I would rather stay home than attend a meeting about meetings.

cards.term: Error: She cannot able to solve it
cards.definition:
Correct: She cannot solve it

Rule: Do not use can and able to together like this.

Example: She cannot solve it yet, but the hint is waiting dramatically.

cards.term: Error: He could able to finish it
cards.definition:
Correct: He could finish it

Rule: Could already expresses ability.

Example: He could finish it if the Wi-Fi stopped pretending to help.

cards.term: Error: I will able to come
cards.definition:
Correct: I will be able to come

Rule: Able needs be after will.

Example: I will be able to come if the train respects the timetable.

cards.term: Error: She must be go there
cards.definition:
Correct: She must go there

Rule: Modal plus base verb, not be plus base verb.

Example: She must go there because the file has chosen her.

cards.term: Error: He may be come
cards.definition:
Correct: He may come

Rule: May is directly followed by base verb.

Example: He may come, but his punctuality has no witnesses.

cards.term: Error: The work is done by him yesterday
cards.definition:
Correct: The work was done by him yesterday

Rule: Use past tense with finished past time.

Example: The work was done yesterday, though the credit arrived today.

cards.term: Error: The letter was wrote by her
cards.definition:
Correct: The letter was written by her

Rule: Passive voice uses be plus V3.

Example: The letter was written by her in handwriting that looked like art.

cards.term: Error: The match is won by India last night
cards.definition:
Correct: The match was won by India last night

Rule: Definite past time needs past tense.

Example: The match was won last night, and the neighbourhood celebrated like a festival.

cards.term: Error: English is speak here
cards.definition:
Correct: English is spoken here

Rule: Passive voice requires past participle.

Example: English is spoken here, but grammar is sometimes negotiated.

cards.term: Error: The road is repairing
cards.definition:
Correct: The road is being repaired

Rule: Passive continuous uses is being plus V3.

Example: The road is being repaired, so the shortcut has become the main road.

cards.term: Error: The bridge was constructing
cards.definition:
Correct: The bridge was being constructed

Rule: Past continuous passive uses was or were being plus V3.

Example: The bridge was being constructed while traffic invented new routes.

cards.term: Error: The food has cooked
cards.definition:
Correct: The food has been cooked

Rule: Perfect passive uses has or have been plus V3.

Example: The food has been cooked, and the smell has already called everyone.

cards.term: Error: The thief has arrested
cards.definition:
Correct: The thief has been arrested

Rule: Passive perfect needs been plus V3.

Example: The thief has been arrested, ending his very short career plan.

cards.term: Error: The work will finish tomorrow
cards.definition:
Correct: The work will be finished tomorrow

Rule: Passive future uses will be plus V3.

Example: The work will be finished tomorrow, according to the most optimistic person in the office.

cards.term: Error: The report should submit today
cards.definition:
Correct: The report should be submitted today

Rule: Passive after modal uses modal plus be plus V3.

Example: The report should be submitted today before the deadline becomes personal.

cards.term: Error: He is born in Delhi
cards.definition:
Correct: He was born in Delhi

Rule: Birth is a past event, so use was born for a living person's birthplace.

Example: He was born in Delhi but argues like he was born in a debate hall.

cards.term: Error: I am born in 2005
cards.definition:
Correct: I was born in 2005

Rule: Use was born for date or year of birth.

Example: I was born in 2005, which my documents repeat more confidently than I do.

cards.term: Error: She has been born in Mumbai
cards.definition:
Correct: She was born in Mumbai

Rule: Use simple past passive for birth.

Example: She was born in Mumbai and still defends its street food like a lawyer.

cards.term: Error: I had gone to school daily
cards.definition:
Correct: I went to school daily

Rule: Past habitual action usually takes simple past, not past perfect.

Example: I went to school daily, though my enthusiasm had weekly holidays.

cards.term: Error: When I was a child, I have played cricket
cards.definition:
Correct: When I was a child, I played cricket

Rule: Use simple past for past habits in a finished period.

Example: When I was a child, I played cricket in lanes narrower than ambition.

cards.term: Error: He would go to temple every morning
cards.definition:
Correct: He used to go to the temple every morning

Rule: Used to is safer for past habits in exam corrections.

Example: He used to go to the temple every morning before office swallowed his schedule.

cards.term: Error: She is going to school every day
cards.definition:
Correct: She goes to school every day

Rule: Daily routines usually use simple present.

Example: She goes to school every day, even when her bag looks heavier than her mood.

cards.term: Error: He is playing cricket every Sunday
cards.definition:
Correct: He plays cricket every Sunday

Rule: Repeated habits use simple present.

Example: He plays cricket every Sunday and discusses it until Monday.

cards.term: Error: The train is leaving at 6 pm tomorrow
cards.definition:
Correct: The train leaves at 6 pm tomorrow

Rule: Fixed timetables often use simple present for future.

Example: The train leaves at 6 pm tomorrow, whether we emotionally accept it or not.

cards.term: Error: The exam will starts at ten
cards.definition:
Correct: The exam will start at ten

Rule: Will is followed by base verb.

Example: The exam will start at ten, and fear will start earlier.

cards.term: Error: He will goes there
cards.definition:
Correct: He will go there

Rule: Will takes base verb.

Example: He will go there if the route has snacks.

cards.term: Error: She will came tomorrow
cards.definition:
Correct: She will come tomorrow

Rule: Will takes V1, not V2.

Example: She will come tomorrow, carrying both notes and judgement.

cards.term: Error: They shall completed the work
cards.definition:
Correct: They shall complete the work

Rule: Shall takes base verb.

Example: They shall complete the work before the supervisor returns.

cards.term: Error: He will be come soon
cards.definition:
Correct: He will come soon

Rule: Do not use be before main verb after will unless forming continuous or passive.

Example: He will come soon, a phrase that often stretches time.

cards.term: Error: I will be waiting when you will arrive
cards.definition:
Correct: I will be waiting when you arrive

Rule: Use present tense in future time clause.

Example: I will be waiting when you arrive, probably beside a dying phone battery.

cards.term: Error: By next year, I will complete the course
cards.definition:
Correct: By next year, I will have completed the course

Rule: Use future perfect for completion before a future time.

Example: By next year, I will have completed the course and collected many abandoned notebooks.

cards.term: Error: By 8 pm, she will finish dinner
cards.definition:
Correct: By 8 pm, she will have finished dinner

Rule: Future perfect shows action completed before a future point.

Example: By 8 pm, she will have finished dinner unless the guests arrive early.

cards.term: Error: By the time you come, I will leave
cards.definition:
Correct: By the time you come, I will have left

Rule: Future perfect shows earlier completion before a future event.

Example: By the time you come, I will have left, because punctuality retired.

cards.term: Error: I will be complete the work
cards.definition:
Correct: I will complete the work

Rule: Will plus base verb is enough for simple future.

Example: I will complete the work, said every student before opening YouTube.

cards.term: Error: I will have been finish the task
cards.definition:
Correct: I will have finished the task

Rule: Future perfect uses will have plus V3.

Example: I will have finished the task before the final reminder arrives.

cards.term: Error: She is gone to market
cards.definition:
Correct: She has gone to the market

Rule: For recent movement with present relevance, use has gone.

Example: She has gone to the market, and the shopping list is now a legal document.

cards.term: Error: He is come back
cards.definition:
Correct: He has come back

Rule: Present perfect uses has plus V3.

Example: He has come back with snacks, so forgiveness is possible.

cards.term: Error: They are returned from Delhi
cards.definition:
Correct: They have returned from Delhi

Rule: Return as active verb uses have returned.

Example: They have returned from Delhi with stories longer than the trip.

cards.term: Error: I am finished my homework
cards.definition:
Correct: I have finished my homework

Rule: Active perfect uses have plus V3, not am plus V3.

Example: I have finished my homework, and even my pen looks shocked.

cards.term: Error: He is completed the project
cards.definition:
Correct: He has completed the project

Rule: Use has plus V3 for active present perfect.

Example: He has completed the project after calling it “almost done” for three days.

cards.term: Error: The train has arrived yesterday
cards.definition:
Correct: The train arrived yesterday

Rule: Finished past time takes simple past.

Example: The train arrived yesterday, late enough to feel traditional.

cards.term: Error: He is suffering from fever since Monday
cards.definition:
Correct: He has been suffering from fever since Monday

Rule: Since plus continuing condition takes present perfect continuous.

Example: He has been suffering from fever since Monday, so jokes can wait.

cards.term: Error: She suffers from fever since Monday
cards.definition:
Correct: She has been suffering from fever since Monday

Rule: Use present perfect continuous for continuing temporary illness.

Example: She has been suffering from fever since Monday and counting tablets like coins.

cards.term: Error: I waited for you since morning
cards.definition:
Correct: I have been waiting for you since morning

Rule: Action continuing to present takes present perfect continuous.

Example: I have been waiting for you since morning, and the bench now knows me.

cards.term: Error: It rained for two hours now
cards.definition:
Correct: It has been raining for two hours now

Rule: “For two hours now” shows action continuing to present.

Example: It has been raining for two hours now, and the road has accepted its new career as a pond.

cards.term: Error: He lives here for ten years now
cards.definition:
Correct: He has lived here for ten years now

Rule: Continuing state from past to present takes present perfect.

Example: He has lived here for ten years now and can identify visitors by footsteps.

cards.term: Error: This is the first time I saw snow
cards.definition:
Correct: This is the first time I have seen snow

Rule: “This is the first time” takes present perfect.

Example: This is the first time I have seen snow outside a wallpaper.

cards.term: Error: It is the best movie I ever saw
cards.definition:
Correct: It is the best movie I have ever seen

Rule: Superlative plus ever often takes present perfect.

Example: It is the best movie I have ever seen, said the person who watched only three.

cards.term: Error: This is the worst food I ever ate
cards.definition:
Correct: This is the worst food I have ever eaten

Rule: Present perfect is used with life experience up to now.

Example: This is the worst food I have ever eaten, and even the spoon looked upset.

cards.term: Error: He is taller than I expected
cards.definition:
Correct: He is taller than I had expected

Rule: Past perfect is often used for an expectation formed before the present comparison.

Example: He is taller than I had expected, which made the group photo complicated.

cards.term: Error: She looks as if she cried
cards.definition:
Correct: She looks as if she has cried

Rule: Present result of a recent past action can take present perfect.

Example: She looks as if she has cried, though she claims it was “just dust”.

cards.term: Error: He talks as if he is knowing everything
cards.definition:
Correct: He talks as if he knows everything

Rule: Know is stative and takes simple present here.

Example: He talks as if he knows everything, including the examiner's lunch menu.

cards.term: Error: He is working in this office for 2019
cards.definition:
Correct: He has been working in this office since 2019

Rule: Since is used for starting point, for is used for duration.

Example: He has been working in this office since 2019, long enough to know the printer's moods.

cards.term: Error: I have lived here since five years
cards.definition:
Correct: I have lived here for five years

Rule: Use for with duration, not since.

Example: I have lived here for five years and still cannot understand the water timing.

cards.term: Error: She has studied since three hours
cards.definition:
Correct: She has studied for three hours

Rule: Use for with duration.

Example: She has studied for three hours, and the highlighter has lost hope.

cards.term: Error: He has been working for Monday
cards.definition:
Correct: He has been working since Monday

Rule: Use since with starting point.

Example: He has been working since Monday, which explains the dangerous silence.

cards.term: Error: I am here since morning
cards.definition:
Correct: I have been here since morning

Rule: State continuing from past to present uses present perfect.

Example: I have been here since morning, and the chair is now emotionally attached.

cards.term: Error: She was knowing the answer
cards.definition:
Correct: She knew the answer

Rule: Know is stative and usually not used in continuous form.

Example: She knew the answer but let others argue for entertainment.

cards.term: Error: I was having a pen
cards.definition:
Correct: I had a pen

Rule: Have meaning possession is not normally continuous.

Example: I had a pen until it joined the mysterious pen disappearance programme.

cards.term: Error: He was believing the rumour
cards.definition:
Correct: He believed the rumour

Rule: Believe is stative.

Example: He believed the rumour because it was forwarded in capital letters.

cards.term: Error: We were understanding the topic
cards.definition:
Correct: We understood the topic

Rule: Understand is usually stative.

Example: We understood the topic right after the test ended.

cards.term: Error: I was seeing that he was wrong
cards.definition:
Correct: I saw that he was wrong

Rule: See meaning understand or realise is stative.

Example: I saw that he was wrong when his confidence outran his facts.

cards.term: Error: The baby cried since morning
cards.definition:
Correct: The baby has been crying since morning

Rule: Continuing action from past to present takes present perfect continuous.

Example: The baby has been crying since morning, and the whole house has surrendered.

cards.term: Error: I have been completed the form
cards.definition:
Correct: I have completed the form

Rule: Active present perfect does not use been before V3.

Example: I have completed the form, which deserves a small celebration.

cards.term: Error: He has been finished the chapter
cards.definition:
Correct: He has finished the chapter

Rule: Use has plus V3 for active perfect.

Example: He has finished the chapter and now speaks like a retired scholar.

cards.term: Error: They had been reached before us
cards.definition:
Correct: They had reached before us

Rule: Active past perfect uses had plus V3, not had been plus V3.

Example: They had reached before us and selected the best seats.

cards.term: Error: She will have been completed the work
cards.definition:
Correct: She will have completed the work

Rule: Future perfect active uses will have plus V3.

Example: She will have completed the work before the deadline starts shouting.

cards.term: Error: The homework has done by me
cards.definition:
Correct: The homework has been done by me

Rule: Passive perfect needs has been plus V3.

Example: The homework has been done by me, after a heroic battle with laziness.

cards.term: Error: He was died in 2010
cards.definition:
Correct: He died in 2010

Rule: Die is an intransitive verb and is not used in passive voice.

Example: He died in 2010, but his poems are still quoted.

cards.term: Error: The accident was happened yesterday
cards.definition:
Correct: The accident happened yesterday

Rule: Happen is intransitive and not used in passive voice.

Example: The accident happened yesterday near the old bridge.

cards.term: Error: The meeting was occurred at noon
cards.definition:
Correct: The meeting occurred at noon

Rule: Occur is intransitive and not passive.

Example: The meeting occurred at noon, though the conclusion did not.

cards.term: Error: The result was appeared online
cards.definition:
Correct: The result appeared online

Rule: Appear is intransitive in this sense.

Example: The result appeared online, and suddenly everyone remembered their roll number.

cards.term: Error: A problem was arisen
cards.definition:
Correct: A problem arose

Rule: Arise is intransitive and not used in passive voice.

Example: A problem arose when the printer met the admit cards.

cards.term: Error: He was slept early
cards.definition:
Correct: He slept early

Rule: Sleep is intransitive and not passive.

Example: He slept early, a rare achievement in exam season.

cards.term: Error: The price was increased yesterday
cards.definition:
Correct: The price increased yesterday

Rule: Increase can be intransitive when no agent is mentioned.

Example: The price increased yesterday, as if wallets needed more drama.

cards.term: Error: The sun was risen
cards.definition:
Correct: The sun rose

Rule: Rise is intransitive and not passive.

Example: The sun rose before the student did.

cards.term: Error: The child was fallen
cards.definition:
Correct: The child fell

Rule: Fall is intransitive and not passive.

Example: The child fell, then looked around to see who noticed.

cards.term: Error: The matter was discussed about
cards.definition:
Correct: The matter was discussed

Rule: Discuss is transitive and does not take about in passive here.

Example: The matter was discussed until even the tea went cold.

cards.term: Error: He discussed about politics
cards.definition:
Correct: He discussed politics

Rule: Discuss is transitive and does not need about.

Example: He discussed politics at dinner and destroyed the peace.

cards.term: Error: She requested for help
cards.definition:
Correct: She requested help

Rule: Request is transitive and usually does not need for before the object.

Example: She requested help after the computer froze at the final step.

cards.term: Error: He entered into the room
cards.definition:
Correct: He entered the room

Rule: Enter meaning go into a place is transitive and does not need into.

Example: He entered the room like he had solved the mystery.

cards.term: Error: They reached to the station
cards.definition:
Correct: They reached the station

Rule: Reach is transitive and does not take to before the place.

Example: They reached the station just as the train tested their faith.

cards.term: Error: He approached to the officer
cards.definition:
Correct: He approached the officer

Rule: Approach is transitive and does not take to before the object.

Example: He approached the officer with a file thicker than confidence.

cards.term: Error: I told to him the truth
cards.definition:
Correct: I told him the truth

Rule: Tell takes a direct object without to.

Example: I told him the truth, and the room became very quiet.

cards.term: Error: He said me the answer
cards.definition:
Correct: He told me the answer

Rule: Say does not take an indirect object this way. Use told.

Example: He told me the answer after the exam, which was not useful.

cards.term: Error: She said that she will come
cards.definition:
Correct: She said that she would come

Rule: In reported speech, will usually changes to would when reporting verb is past.

Example: She said that she would come, and everyone began calculating delay.

cards.term: Error: He said that he is ill
cards.definition:
Correct: He said that he was ill

Rule: Present tense changes to past in reported speech after past reporting verb.

Example: He said that he was ill, but his cricket photos disagreed.

cards.term: Error: She told that she was busy
cards.definition:
Correct: She said that she was busy

Rule: Tell needs an object. Say can be used without personal object.

Example: She said that she was busy, which usually means no.

cards.term: Error: He told me that he will help
cards.definition:
Correct: He told me that he would help

Rule: Will changes to would in indirect speech after past reporting verb.

Example: He told me that he would help, then disappeared like free Wi-Fi.

cards.term: Error: He asked me where do I live
cards.definition:
Correct: He asked me where I lived

Rule: Indirect questions use statement word order and backshift.

Example: He asked me where I lived, not where do I live.

cards.term: Error: She asked why was I late
cards.definition:
Correct: She asked why I was late

Rule: Indirect questions do not use question word order.

Example: She asked why I was late, and traffic received all the blame.

cards.term: Error: He asked me did I finish it
cards.definition:
Correct: He asked me whether I had finished it

Rule: Yes/no indirect questions use whether or if and statement order.

Example: He asked me whether I had finished it, and my silence answered first.

cards.term: Error: She asked me what I am doing
cards.definition:
Correct: She asked me what I was doing

Rule: Present continuous changes to past continuous in reported speech.

Example: She asked me what I was doing, and “studying” sounded ambitious.

cards.term: Error: He said that honesty is the best policy
cards.definition:
Correct: He said that honesty is the best policy

Rule: Universal truths do not need tense change in reported speech.

Example: He said that honesty is the best policy, which is still true after exams.

cards.term: Error: The teacher said that the earth moved around the sun
cards.definition:
Correct: The teacher said that the earth moves around the sun

Rule: Scientific truths remain in present tense.

Example: The teacher said that the earth moves around the sun, not around our excuses.

cards.term: Error: I wish I have worked harder
cards.definition:
Correct: I wish I had worked harder

Rule: Wish about past regret uses had plus V3.

Example: I wish I had worked harder, said the student after meeting the answer key.

cards.term: Error: If only I know the answer
cards.definition:
Correct: If only I knew the answer

Rule: If only for present wish uses past tense.

Example: If only I knew the answer, I would stop staring at option B.

cards.term: Error: If only he has listened
cards.definition:
Correct: If only he had listened

Rule: If only for past regret uses had plus V3.

Example: If only he had listened, the charger would still be alive.

cards.term: Error: He talks as though he owns the place
cards.definition:
Correct: He talks as though he owned the place

Rule: Unreal comparison can take past tense.

Example: He talks as though he owned the place, including the air.

cards.term: Error: She acts as if she has never made a mistake
cards.definition:
Correct: She acts as if she had never made a mistake

Rule: Unreal past idea after as if may use past perfect.

Example: She acts as if she had never made a mistake, which is historically inaccurate.

cards.term: Error: It is high time we leave
cards.definition:
Correct: It is high time we left

Rule: High time is followed by past tense.

Example: It is high time we left before the meeting grows another agenda.

cards.term: Error: I would rather he stays here
cards.definition:
Correct: I would rather he stayed here

Rule: Would rather plus subject takes past tense for present preference.

Example: I would rather he stayed here, because his “quick trips” are never quick.

cards.term: Error: He behaves as if he is rich
cards.definition:
Correct: He behaves as if he were rich

Rule: Unreal present after as if takes past subjunctive.

Example: He behaves as if he were rich, but his wallet has objections.

cards.term: Error: No sooner he reached than it started raining
cards.definition:
Correct: No sooner did he reach than it started raining

Rule: No sooner at the beginning takes inversion with did.

Example: No sooner did he reach than it started raining like a planned attack.

cards.term: Error: Hardly he had reached when the bell rang
cards.definition:
Correct: Hardly had he reached when the bell rang

Rule: Hardly at the beginning takes inversion.

Example: Hardly had he reached when the bell rang and rescued the class.

cards.term: Error: Scarcely he entered when everyone stood up
cards.definition:
Correct: Scarcely had he entered when everyone stood up

Rule: Scarcely at the beginning takes inversion with had.

Example: Scarcely had he entered when everyone stood up in sudden discipline.

cards.term: Error: Not only he sings but also dances
cards.definition:
Correct: Not only does he sing but he also dances

Rule: Not only at the beginning takes inversion in the first clause.

Example: Not only does he sing, but he also dances like the stage owes him money.

cards.term: Error: Seldom I have seen such courage
cards.definition:
Correct: Seldom have I seen such courage

Rule: Negative adverbs at the beginning often take inversion.

Example: Seldom have I seen such courage in a school debate.

cards.term: Error: Never I saw such a sight
cards.definition:
Correct: Never have I seen such a sight

Rule: Never at the beginning takes inversion.

Example: Never have I seen such a sight, except maybe during exam-result week.

cards.term: Error: Only then I understood the rule
cards.definition:
Correct: Only then did I understand the rule

Rule: Only then at the beginning takes inversion.

Example: Only then did I understand the rule, after losing one mark to it.

cards.term: Error: Not until he came I left
cards.definition:
Correct: Not until he came did I leave

Rule: Not until at the beginning requires inversion in the main clause.

Example: Not until he came did I leave, because someone had to guard the snacks.

cards.term: Error: Neither he helped nor he apologised
cards.definition:
Correct: Neither did he help nor did he apologise

Rule: Negative paired structure often uses inversion.

Example: Neither did he help nor did he apologise, a complete package of disappointment.

cards.term: Error: Rarely he speaks in class
cards.definition:
Correct: Rarely does he speak in class

Rule: Rarely at the beginning takes inversion.

Example: Rarely does he speak in class, so everyone listens when he does.

cards.term: Error: I am having a headache since morning
cards.definition:
Correct: I have had a headache since morning

Rule: Have meaning experience of illness can use present perfect for duration.

Example: I have had a headache since morning, and the construction noise is applying for credit.

cards.term: Error: The shop opens since 1990
cards.definition:
Correct: The shop has been open since 1990

Rule: Use present perfect for a state continuing from a past point.

Example: The shop has been open since 1990 and still uses the same calculator.

cards.term: Error: He is dead for ten years
cards.definition:
Correct: He has been dead for ten years

Rule: Use present perfect for a state continuing for a duration.

Example: He has been dead for ten years, but his songs still travel everywhere.

cards.term: Error: They are married since 2010
cards.definition:
Correct: They have been married since 2010

Rule: Use present perfect for a state continuing from a point in time.

Example: They have been married since 2010 and still debate the TV remote.

cards.term: Error: He is ill for a week
cards.definition:
Correct: He has been ill for a week

Rule: Use present perfect for a state continuing for a duration.

Example: He has been ill for a week, and the medicine shelf looks busier than usual.

cards.term: Error: The door is open since morning
cards.definition:
Correct: The door has been open since morning

Rule: Use present perfect for continuing state.

Example: The door has been open since morning, and mosquitoes treated it as an invitation.

cards.term: Error: I am here for two hours
cards.definition:
Correct: I have been here for two hours

Rule: Continuing state from past to present takes present perfect.

Example: I have been here for two hours, and patience has left without me.

cards.term: Error: He has gone to Delhi and returned yesterday
cards.definition:
Correct: He went to Delhi and returned yesterday

Rule: Use simple past for completed actions at a definite past time.

Example: He went to Delhi and returned yesterday with stories, receipts, and dust.

cards.term: Error: She has been to market yesterday
cards.definition:
Correct: She went to the market yesterday

Rule: Yesterday requires simple past.

Example: She went to the market yesterday and returned with everything except what was needed.

cards.term: Error: I have seen him in 2018
cards.definition:
Correct: I saw him in 2018

Rule: Specific past year takes simple past.

Example: I saw him in 2018, back when the notes were still fresh.

cards.term: Error: We have visited the museum last week
cards.definition:
Correct: We visited the museum last week

Rule: Last week is a finished past time.

Example: We visited the museum last week and learned that old coins can be exciting.

cards.term: Error: She has never went there
cards.definition:
Correct: She has never gone there

Rule: Never with present perfect still needs V3.

Example: She has never gone there, though she gives directions confidently.

cards.term: Error: I had never saw such courage
cards.definition:
Correct: I had never seen such courage

Rule: Past perfect requires V3.

Example: I had never seen such courage before the small child faced the stage.

cards.term: Error: He has already did the work
cards.definition:
Correct: He has already done the work

Rule: Already with present perfect takes V3.

Example: He has already done the work, which made the reminder message unnecessary.

cards.term: Error: They had already ate dinner
cards.definition:
Correct: They had already eaten dinner

Rule: Had already is followed by V3.

Example: They had already eaten dinner before the guests arrived with more food.

cards.term: Error: She has just came
cards.definition:
Correct: She has just come

Rule: Just with present perfect takes V3.

Example: She has just come, and the room has immediately become louder.

cards.term: Error: I have just wrote it
cards.definition:
Correct: I have just written it

Rule: Have just takes past participle.

Example: I have just written it, and the ink is still emotionally fresh.

cards.term: Error: He has yet not arrived
cards.definition:
Correct: He has not arrived yet

Rule: Correct placement is not plus verb plus yet at the end.

Example: He has not arrived yet, which surprises absolutely nobody.

cards.term: Error: I didn't went because I was ill
cards.definition:
Correct: I didn't go because I was ill

Rule: Did not takes base verb.

Example: I didn't go because I was ill, not because the test looked dangerous.

cards.term: Error: Did she came on time?
cards.definition:
Correct: Did she come on time?

Rule: Did takes base verb.

Example: Did she come on time, or did time come and leave?

cards.term: Error: Why did he left early?
cards.definition:
Correct: Why did he leave early?

Rule: Did plus subject plus base verb.

Example: Why did he leave early, just before the bill arrived?

cards.term: Error: Where did you kept the keys?
cards.definition:
Correct: Where did you keep the keys?

Rule: Did is followed by V1.

Example: Where did you keep the keys, and why is the sofa looking guilty?

cards.term: Error: I did not meant that
cards.definition:
Correct: I did not mean that

Rule: Did not takes base verb.

Example: I did not mean that, said the person after meaning exactly that.

cards.term: Error: He do not knows me
cards.definition:
Correct: He does not know me

Rule: Singular third person uses does not plus V1.

Example: He does not know me, but his dog clearly remembers me.

cards.term: Error: She do not comes here
cards.definition:
Correct: She does not come here

Rule: Use does not with singular subject and base verb.

Example: She does not come here unless someone mentions sweets.

cards.term: Error: It do not make sense
cards.definition:
Correct: It does not make sense

Rule: It takes does not.

Example: It does not make sense, which is why it resembles office paperwork.

cards.term: Error: They does not want help
cards.definition:
Correct: They do not want help

Rule: Plural subject uses do not.

Example: They do not want help until the deadline appears.

cards.term: Error: We does not accept this
cards.definition:
Correct: We do not accept this

Rule: We takes do not.

Example: We do not accept this answer without proof.

cards.term: Error: I does not agree
cards.definition:
Correct: I do not agree

Rule: I takes do not.

Example: I do not agree, but I am willing to hear the wrong argument.
